# UI/UX design: inclusive systems — facts

## Structure and components

- [statement] GOV.UK’s contribution criteria make inclusive evidence part of publication readiness: components must work in research with a representative sample including users with disabilities, and across browsers, assistive technologies and devices. The criteria also require clarity about the contexts actually tested. (low confidence) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Preply’s practitioner account distinguishes coverage (usage) from adoption (correct usage). It also tracks documentation, platform parity and user feedback, so a usage increase alone should not be reported as proof of correct component use or system quality. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] UXPin recommends explicit approval rights for components, variants, breaking changes and exceptions, plus a logged exception path with an expiry date or migration plan. (low confidence) — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-system-governance/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] UXPin describes a component lifecycle from proposal through review, build, documentation, release, adoption measurement and deprecation; it asks for use-case and reuse evidence before adding variants. (low confidence) — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-system-governance/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] In Curtis’s spec-driven approach, component specifications describe the public API, variant rules and composed examples; supplemental requirements capture behavior, accessibility and state precedence such as `disabled` over `read-only`. (low confidence) — https://nathanacurtis.substack.com/p/spec-driven-ui-component-development · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Communicate component retirement before removal: GOV.UK describes deprecation as advance notice of a future breaking change, while zeroheight warns that deleting an in-use component immediately can leave gaps and lost references. (medium confidence) — https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/v5/staying-up-to-date/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle · also: https://help.zeroheight.com/hc/en-us/articles/36474257606555-Deprecating-in-design-systems-When-it-s-time-to-say-goodbye
- [statement] zeroheight recommends inspecting component dependencies and replacement fit before retirement: check direct template usage, nesting in larger components, whether replacements differ by use case, and whether contained components also become redundant. (low confidence) — https://help.zeroheight.com/hc/en-us/articles/36474257606555-Deprecating-in-design-systems-When-it-s-time-to-say-goodbye · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Preply explicitly avoids mandatory visual-coverage targets: bespoke needs and third-party components can justify lower coverage. Its account also warns that popular public pages can obscure other teams in aggregate measurements. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] A composite token contains named subvalues for related styling properties applied together; it is not merely an arbitrary group of independently organized tokens. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Resolve aliases after context selection and ordered overrides have produced the final token structure. The resolver allows deep alias chains but forbids circular references and requires the referenced type to match. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] DTCG composite tokens combine multiple named sub-values in a predefined structure. Tokens Studio distinguishes these from its legacy generic composition token, which its guide recommends replacing with independently defined token types. (high confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes · also: https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-types/composition
- [statement] Resolver ordering is significant: later sets or selected modifier contexts override earlier conflicting tokens. Aliases must resolve after the ordered token structure has been flattened. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Handoff specifications should make states and responsive behavior explicit. The developers interviewed by zeroheight describe missing intermediate-width behavior, long-content rules, and empty states; Figma’s guide describes component documentation that includes variants and states. (medium confidence) — https://zeroheight.com/blog/what-do-developers-want-in-a-design-handoff-we-asked-them/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/
- [statement] Plan accessible venues or remote participation, transportation, breaks and usable materials as part of recruitment logistics; budget participant payments and access-related expenses. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] W3C recommends tightly wrapping each opposite-direction inline phrase, setting its base direction, and preserving nested directional structure. Directional isolation prevents the phrase from influencing surrounding text; unknown-direction content needs automatic direction determination and isolation. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Figma distinguishes user flows, which map user actions and decisions, from task flows focused on a single action and wireframes focused on interface layout and structure. These artifacts answer different design questions. (low confidence) — https://www.figma.com/resource-library/user-flow/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity
- [statement] A wireframe can make screen structure and layout testable without finished visual details. It should not be interpreted as evidence about every visual attribute of a finished interface. (medium confidence) — https://www.figma.com/resource-library/user-flow/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-prototype-hi-lo-fidelity/

## How it works

- [statement] Reduce memory demands by making process position and instructions visible: COGA recommends showing completed, current and pending steps, while Coforma recommends persistent instructions throughout multi-step processes. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX · also: https://coforma.io/perspectives/give-users-brains-a-break-ux-tips-for-cognitive-accessibility?utm_source=title2info&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=07142025&utm_content=editorial
- [statement] COGA recommends authentication alternatives that do not require memorizing strings, calculations, copying content, puzzles, reproducing gestures, or transcribing displayed characters; these are design recommendations, not a claim that every authentication mechanism must have identical cognitive demands. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends avoiding timeouts and letting users save work as they go. If that is impossible, explain the available time and whether a timeout will discard entered data when the process begins. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] GOV.UK Frontend v5 guidance uses patch increments for bug fixes, minor increments for new features and major increments for potentially required consumer changes; it still directs consumers to read release notes and test upgrades because breaking impact depends on usage. (low confidence) — https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/v5/staying-up-to-date/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] GOV.UK publication criteria require evidence from a representative sample including users with disabilities; limited deployment is acceptable when tested contexts are stated and wider feedback is encouraged. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Cross-platform conversion can lose responsive typography behavior: the DTCG dimension definition permits a lossy fixed-size conversion when a target platform has no equivalent to relative root-font sizing. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Mila Cann argues against discrete handoffs in agile teams because they imply design is finished; Cegid instead uses handoff to mean a transition into shared implementation responsibility. These are explicitly attributed process framings, not evidence that implementation documentation should be eliminated. (medium confidence) — https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/design-handoffs-dont-belong-in-agile-environments-61abba8e7848 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/
- [statement] Make implementation-ready work distinguishable from drafts and experiments. Figma describes separating work by readiness; zeroheight records developer difficulty identifying the authoritative design among experiments. (medium confidence) — https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://zeroheight.com/blog/what-do-developers-want-in-a-design-handoff-we-asked-them/
- [statement] Keep designers and developers engaged during delivery. Cegid recommends resolving implementation edge cases together; Figma describes early, frequent sharing as a way to obtain feedback before the end of the process. These are practitioner recommendations, not quantified causal estimates. (medium confidence) — https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/
- [statement] Modeinspect recommends actionable QA findings that record location, expected value, observed value, severity, and a screenshot. When an engineer fixes a finding through a comment or ticket, its workflow includes a second designer review of the updated build. (low confidence) — https://modeinspect.com/blog/design-qa · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] Disability advocacy groups, community organizations and specialist accessibility panels provide recruitment channels. When using an agency, check its disability recruitment experience and specify the actual access needs relevant to the study. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/
- [statement] Treat consent as continuing: remind participants that participation is voluntary and check again when they appear uncomfortable or confused; allow withdrawal without forfeiting the promised incentive. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Explain any practical cutoff for withdrawing already anonymised or published data. Cambridge’s Inclusive Design Toolkit specifically advises disclosing when later withdrawal becomes impossible. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Offer consent materials in usable formats and provide a documented verbal-consent route when appropriate; a handwritten signature is not the only way these guides describe recording consent. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Explain that participation is voluntary and withdrawal is permitted; GOV.UK additionally advises checking continued consent when a participant seems uncomfortable or confused. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] The guides scope post-session withdrawal differently: GOV.UK prescribes deletion on withdrawal, while Cambridge explicitly addresses limits after anonymisation or repository publication. Treat these as attributed guidance and explain the study-specific withdrawal process and limits in advance. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Treat text alignment and text direction as separate design decisions. Material Design distinguishes the placement of a text box from the flow within it and identifies text entry, cursor position, punctuation, phone numbers and URLs as common RTL rendering trouble spots. (low confidence) — https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Do not reverse the digits inside a number when adapting an interface to RTL. Numeral shapes can still vary by locale; number localization and digit-order reversal are separate decisions. (medium confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/right-to-left · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html
- [statement] Validate the meaning and tone of localized content through user tasks, including when different markets share a language. Nielsen Norman Group recommends content testing with culturally diverse audiences and reviewing tone after translation. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-international-usability-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Participation can remain tokenistic despite an invitation: participants in the empirical framework reported that their input was ignored and management merely claimed it had involved disabled people. NPC recommends active input throughout the process and freedom to disagree with facilitators. (high confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.thinknpc.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Co-design-guidance-July-2019.pdf
- [statement] For the boundary between flow diagrams and detailed specifications, practitioner Michael Lai proposes high-level task flows plus annotated detailed designs for deviations or new interaction patterns, so developers can resolve questions without detailing every familiar interaction. (low confidence) — https://ux.stackexchange.com/questions/137052/should-i-cover-every-single-user-flow-including-error-states-in-wireframes-for-w · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use clear, concrete language and examples; keep content concise without losing precision. Both COGA and the AASPIRE guidelines recommend this approach. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] Use COGA alongside WCAG to address cognitive usability needs beyond conformance; W3C explicitly describes COGA patterns as supplemental guidance, and DWP recommends cross-referencing them when improving services beyond AA. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX · also: https://dwpdigital.blog.gov.uk/2022/06/30/designing-accessible-services-dont-exclude-the-neurodiverse/
- [statement] Use data within the consent obtained, minimize personal data collection, protect stored data and explain sharing and recordings to participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research
- [statement] Check locale-specific date formats, currency placement, decimal and grouping separators, measurement units, address forms and phone validation. SimpleLocalize lists these as localization QA checks. (low confidence) — https://simplelocalize.io/blog/posts/ui-localization-best-practices/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Limit interruptions and distracting motion, and provide user controls: COGA recommends control over interruptions and content changes, and AASPIRE recommends avoiding moving images and decorative visual or sonic clutter. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] Fable cautions that automated checks cannot determine whether language is confusing, steps feel overwhelming or navigation is predictable; its article recommends validation by people with lived cognitive-accessibility experience. (low confidence) — https://makeitfable.com/article/cognitive-accessibility-pilot-case-study/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] DWP cautions against treating blanket AAA conformance as a universal solution, noting that some content cannot satisfy every AAA criterion; its recommended approach is to consider useful AAA criteria and cross-reference COGA patterns and user stories. (low confidence) — https://dwpdigital.blog.gov.uk/2022/06/30/designing-accessible-services-dont-exclude-the-neurodiverse/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] Matan Rosen recommends component specifications that enumerate states and variants, anatomy, boundaries, empty and error states, text constraints and keyboard interactions. This makes behavior and limits explicit alongside appearance. (low confidence) — https://uxdesign.cc/component-spec-the-design-system-component-delivery-5f88db6ccf7e · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Capozzi’s migration account identifies a coordination failure mode: automatic replacement leaves special cases that require consuming teams’ knowledge and roadmap capacity. Its numerical automation estimates are the author’s guesses, so they should not become general migration benchmarks. (low confidence) — https://maecapozzi.com/newsletter/75 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Resolver portability has a boundary: same-document references are mandatory, but tools may decline local-file or remote-URI imports. Bundling through optional definitions can also fail to transfer across tools that ignore those definitions. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] In Weblate issue 5340, a maintainer attributed an apparent Arabic punctuation displacement to stored character order and rendering context, and advised checking the consuming application. This historical support exchange illustrates why a JSON preview alone cannot establish correct bidi behavior. (low confidence) — https://github.com/WeblateOrg/weblate/issues/5340 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Test contraction as well as expansion, and inspect long unbreakable compounds. W3C notes that smaller translations can leave problematic whitespace and that compound words can fail to wrap where an English phrase wraps. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Do not generalize one disabled participant’s input to everyone. W3C warns that experience varies even within one disability; user involvement must be combined with accessibility standards and conformance evaluation because participants cannot cover all disabilities and assistive-technology configurations. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/WAI/planning/involving-users/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design
- [statement] In a UX Stack Exchange practitioner account, leaving error states and secondary screens until high-fidelity prototyping led to missing screens and user dead ends. The author later reported that covering error flows in wireframes saved team effort; this is an experience report, not a measured universal effect. (low confidence) — https://ux.stackexchange.com/questions/137052/should-i-cover-every-single-user-flow-including-error-states-in-wireframes-for-w · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity
- [statement] Walker, Takayama and Landay found few differences in the number, type and severity of usability issues across paper/computer and low/high-fidelity website prototypes in their experiment. MeasuringU’s review likewise supports low-fidelity prototypes for finding major issues, while warning they are imperfect substitutes. This supports early issue discovery, not equivalence for every test outcome. (medium confidence) — https://www.leilatakayama.org/downloads/Takayama.Prototypes_HFES2002_prepress.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity · also: https://measuringu.com/prototype-fidelity/
- [statement] GOV.UK warns that an online alpha prototype cannot support the full range of technical accessibility tests used for production code. Prototype findings therefore leave a specific validation boundary for the later implementation. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-alpha-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] To support task preparation and planning, COGA recommends stating the expected effort, required resources and process overview before a multi-step task, and making in-progress versus completed status clear. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] Provide presentation choices rather than assume one display suits everyone: COGA recommends font, spacing and contrast preferences, and AASPIRE recommends color-palette choices and both smaller and larger fonts. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/
- [statement] AASPIRE developed its guidelines through iterative autistic end-user involvement and empirically evaluated the resulting website; this is evidence about that intervention rather than proof that every recommendation works for every neurodivergent user. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] In Fable’s pilot, some participants needed to complete tasks silently before explaining their thoughts, so its authors recommend offering a do-first option rather than requiring concurrent think-aloud; this is a pilot-specific observation, not a general incapacity attributed to neurodivergent users. (low confidence) — https://makeitfable.com/article/cognitive-accessibility-pilot-case-study/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] Design around functional needs rather than assuming a diagnosis determines a person’s interface needs. Fable recommends a needs-based approach, including people without formal diagnoses; W3C identifies memory, attention, processing, language, and learning barriers as distinct design concerns. (medium confidence) — https://makeitfable.com/article/cognitive-accessibility-pilot-case-study/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Société Générale’s practitioner account describes a council that checks consistency, reviews documentation and supports contributions. Council membership depends on available time and enthusiasm; this is a contextual operating model rather than evidence that one structure fits every organization. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/societe-generale-design/taming-design-system-chaos-66bcadbf43e1 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Nathan Curtis argues that federation should augment dedicated central capacity rather than replace it. His practitioner account describes a stalled system after the responsible team was disbanded without relieving federated contributors of their existing responsibilities; it is not a controlled comparison of governance models. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/@nathanacurtis/the-fallacy-of-federated-design-systems-23b9a9a05542 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Deprecation should include a transition plan and visibility into consumption rather than immediate deletion. Zeroheight recommends communication and usage analysis; Mae Capozzi describes replacement parity, preventing new deprecated uses, automation and product-team help for cases requiring manual migration. (medium confidence) — https://help.zeroheight.com/hc/en-us/articles/36474257606555-Deprecating-in-design-systems-When-it-s-time-to-say-goodbye · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle · also: https://maecapozzi.com/newsletter/75
- [statement] Preply describes visual coverage as a measure of design-system usage in rendered products, complementing static code analysis. Its account says coverage is one metric among several and is a diagnostic signal rather than a score teams must maximize. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] Preply distinguishes codebase usage from what users actually encounter; its visual coverage measures use of design-system components in products, rather than proving correct usage. (low confidence) — https://medium.com/preply-engineering/visual-coverage-why-and-how-preply-measures-the-impact-of-the-design-system-1057115f4aff · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] UXPin presents governance structure as a tradeoff: a small or overloaded central team can bottleneck contributions, while federated contributions require communication and coordination and may introduce inconsistency when guidelines are not followed. (low confidence) — https://www.uxpin.com/studio/blog/design-system-governance/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] DTCG defines a platform-agnostic interchange format for design decisions; its purpose is to reduce bespoke integrations between design and development tools, rather than prescribe a particular authoring tool. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Contentful distinguishes modes as variations within token collections and defines a theme, in its own model, as a separate complete token set retaining the same structure. Treat this as an attributed convention rather than a universal definition of themes. (low confidence) — https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Tokens Studio documents a concrete composition limit: applying a composition token styles one layer rather than all child layers, and individual property tokens attached to Figma styles or variables do not appear as such in the Figma UI. (low confidence) — https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-types/composition · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Contentful uses mode for contextual value variations, collection for tokens that share modes, and theme for the full set of collections; the article cautions that theme is also sometimes used to mean mode. These are the article’s working definitions rather than universal interchange terminology. (low confidence) — https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] GDS recommends accessibility acceptance criteria that are specific, testable, and expressed as outcomes rather than prescribed solutions. In its method, criteria preserve earlier accessibility decisions and evolve when implementation or testing reveals missing needs. (low confidence) — https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/01/24/improving-accessibility-with-accessibility-acceptance-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] GOV.UK explicitly cautions that accessibility acceptance criteria alone do not make a service accessible; use them to preserve accessibility decisions across iterations rather than treating a completed checklist as sufficient assurance. (low confidence) — https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/01/24/improving-accessibility-with-accessibility-acceptance-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] Handoff documentation should preserve the problem and decision context, rather than conveying only final screens: Figma describes a spec containing iterations, problem definitions, research links, and documentation; developers interviewed by zeroheight report missing the reasons and trade-offs behind designs. (medium confidence) — https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://zeroheight.com/blog/what-do-developers-want-in-a-design-handoff-we-asked-them/
- [statement] NN/g explicitly cautions that not every interface inconsistency is UX debt: temporary intentional variations, such as an experiment, can be acceptable when they do not cause user problems. This scopes debt triage to experience harm rather than treating every visual difference as a defect. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-debt/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] For disability-inclusive recruitment, specify functional access needs, assistive technology and devices rather than relying on diagnosis labels; match recruitment criteria to likely barriers in the product. (medium confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group cautions that convenience samples, coworkers and existing-customer panels can bias feedback or omit new-user perspectives; select channels against the study question rather than convenience alone. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recruiting-screening-research-candidates/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] For children, adults with consent-related support needs, or methods where ordinary consent is impractical, consult specific ethical guidance and the rules of the relevant countries rather than extending a generic UX consent template uncritically. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Section508.gov advises screening for functional needs, assistive technology, typical devices and technology comfort rather than medical diagnoses. (low confidence) — https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Budget participant compensation and participation costs rather than treating access expenses as incidental: Cambridge recommends reimbursing out-of-pocket costs, while Section508.gov includes incentives, travel support and separate attendant reimbursement. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Great Question cautions that much academic incentive-bias research concerns surveys and clinical trials rather than moderated UX interviews; this limits direct generalization to UX sessions. (low confidence) — https://www.greatquestion.com/blog/how-do-incentives-impact-bias-in-ux-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] The Material Design versions differ in stated scope: Material Design 2 describes linear time as mirrored in RTL, whereas Material Design 3 explicitly keeps Hebrew linear progress indicators LTR. Apply the version- and locale-specific guidance rather than treating the older generalization as universal. (low confidence) — https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl
- [statement] Agree the aims, limits of influence and decision process with participants at the outset. Document collaboration terms in a written agreement, rather than inviting people only after options are polished. (high confidence) — https://www.thinknpc.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Co-design-guidance-July-2019.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952, https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Include people with lived experience early and throughout the process, and consider roles on the project team or as workshop co-facilitators rather than restricting them to late feedback. (medium confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Remote co-design can remove travel demands while introducing inaccessible collaboration tools and connectivity barriers. Select the format around participants’ access needs rather than assuming that moving online makes a workshop accessible. (medium confidence) — https://maitraye.github.io/files/posters/Remote-Codesign-workshop-ASSETS22.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Johansson and colleagues explicitly frame their participation framework around impact rather than control, and argue that the quality of participation can be assessed by measures other than power. This scopes stronger claims that co-design always requires maximal participant control. (low confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design
- [statement] Plan accessibility across activities, materials and communication, rather than treating venue access as sufficient. The empirical framework describes reading text aloud, sign-language interpreting and slowing discussion; Alfred Health also budgets accessible information, interpreters and spaces meeting physical and sensory needs. (high confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Figma recommends defining the user goal, entry point, meaningful steps, decision points and success endpoint. Its decision-point guidance explicitly includes error messages and alternative paths, so a flow should represent relevant exceptions rather than only a successful route. (low confidence) — https://www.figma.com/resource-library/user-flow/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity
- [statement] Scope prototypes around learning: GOV.UK advises focusing alpha prototypes on the most challenging areas to test risky assumptions, rather than necessarily building the entire journey. Ontario describes alpha as testing hypotheses and trying approaches with users before building a service. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-alpha-phase-works · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity · also: https://github.com/ongov/Service-Design-Playbook
- [statement] GOV.UK recommends code prototypes for realistic service interactions, but says prototype code need not meet production security or traffic-performance standards and must not simply be copied into production. Its alpha guidance similarly calls for testing code rather than production-quality implementation. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/making-prototypes · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity · also: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-alpha-phase-works, https://prototype-kit.service.gov.uk/prototyping/
- [statement] GOV.UK recommends code prototypes for realistic service research; Walker and colleagues found low- and high-fidelity prototypes equally good at uncovering usability issues in their experiment. The positions address different scopes: realistic interaction versus issue discovery in the tested websites. Neither establishes that one fidelity is best for every research question. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/making-prototypes · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity · also: https://www.leilatakayama.org/downloads/Takayama.Prototypes_HFES2002_prepress.pdf
- [statement] Fidelity has separable dimensions such as interaction, visual appearance and content. Presentation medium is also a separate choice: paper versus computer should not be treated as equivalent to low versus high fidelity. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-prototype-hi-lo-fidelity/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity · also: https://www.leilatakayama.org/downloads/Takayama.Prototypes_HFES2002_prepress.pdf
- [statement] Pilot a prototype before study sessions. NN/G warns that a wrong screen or slow simulated response can alter user expectations and interpretation; when an action has no prepared response, it recommends asking what the participant expected rather than explaining how the design should work. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-prototype-hi-lo-fidelity/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Task flows, wireframes and prototype fidelity

## Facts and statements

- [statement] W3C COGA Content Usable provides supplemental guidance beyond WCAG requirements; following it is not required for WCAG conformance. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends placing clear, concise instructions before or beside the activity, breaking them into complete steps, and supplying examples or illustrations. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends reducing unnecessary decisions and steps: keep required workflows to their minimally necessary steps and separate optional actions, to reduce distractions, mistakes, and mental fatigue. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends that context, functionality and settings changes be user initiated or have an easy off switch, together with an easy way to return to the previous state. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] Scope AASPIRE findings to their study context: the authors identify a simple informational website, a convenience evaluation sample, and primarily non-Hispanic white participants as limits. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6485264/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends making the page purpose and position within a task recognizable, including after a user loses focus. Its user stories explicitly connect these orientation needs with attention, memory, and executive-function impairments. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends an easy way to control interruptions, reminders, and changing content, except user-initiated events or emergencies; it describes pause controls and user-selected interruption settings as attention and memory supports. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] COGA recommends supporting personalization and simplification without disabling add-ons or extensions, including spelling support, password support, text-to-speech, and synchronized highlighting. It also recommends user-initiated context changes or an easy off switch, plus a way back to the previous context. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Cognitive accessibility and neuroinclusive UX
- [statement] Contribution governance can separate proposal eligibility from publication readiness: GOV.UK checks usefulness and uniqueness before reviewing usability, consistency and versatility; Société Générale describes a single request entry point with council triage and explicit outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle · also: https://medium.com/societe-generale-design/taming-design-system-chaos-66bcadbf43e1
- [statement] GOV.UK Frontend v5 documents deprecation as advance notice of a future breaking change, usually in the next major version. Addressing deprecations incrementally reduces the work needed for a later major upgrade. (low confidence) — https://frontend.design-system.service.gov.uk/v5/staying-up-to-date/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] GOV.UK’s August 2026 research on prototype lifecycle labels found that “Trial” was broadly understood, while “Needs review” created uncertainty about onward use. Participants wanted context about accessibility testing and future changes. The findings support explaining what each label means and what action users should take; they do not establish that these proposed labels were deployed. (low confidence) — https://github.com/alphagov/govuk-design-system/discussions/5622 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] GOV.UK contribution guidance separates proposal review for usefulness and uniqueness from implementation review for usability, consistency and versatility. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-08) — https://design-system.service.gov.uk/community/contribution-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design system governance and component lifecycle
- [statement] The DTCG Format Module 2025.10 is a stable Community Group specification, explicitly neither a W3C Standard nor on the W3C Standards Track. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] In the DTCG format, a token type may be explicit or derived from a referenced token or the closest typed parent group; an undeterminable type is invalid, and tools must not guess it from the value. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Aliases let semantic names reference underlying tokens. Contentful and Aha! illustrate keeping usage-oriented names stable while changing the primitive values selected for a theme. (high confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes · also: https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/, https://www.aha.io/engineering/articles/design-tokens-the-building-blocks-of-a-design-system
- [statement] The resolver explicitly covers light, dark and high-contrast color modes, sizing contexts, and accessibility contexts such as reduced motion; it addresses repeated token values across combinations of contexts. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] In the DTCG resolver, sets provide token sources and modifiers conditionally select sources through named contexts. Later sources override earlier occurrences, and the resolution order determines the final tokens. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] The format requires tools to preserve extension data they do not understand, but recommends keeping extensions to optional metadata that is not essential to interpreting a token value. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Resolver conformance does not guarantee remote-file interoperability: same-document references are required, while tools may decline local-file or remote-network URI types. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Tokens Studio distinguishes its legacy generic composition token from specifically typed composite tokens. Its documentation recommends migration and describes difficult code transformations and known composition-token bugs; this documents a portability hazard, not a verified status of every linked bug. (low confidence) — https://docs.tokens.studio/manage-tokens/token-types/composition · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] In a 2024 Style Dictionary discussion, collaborator `jorenbroekema` recommends theme-specific semantic overrides and separate outputs for scalability, while requester lukasoppermann says manual file management is burdensome and unused CSS is not a major concern for that project. These are conflicting workflow judgments, not measured universal performance results. (low confidence) — https://github.com/style-dictionary/style-dictionary/issues/1171 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Design tokens express design decisions independently of a target platform; an interchange file still needs translation into platform-specific outputs. (high confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes · also: https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/
- [statement] The DTCG Format Module defines a JSON interchange format intended to reduce bespoke integrations between token tools. Its publication status explicitly says it is not a W3C Standard. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Aliases let a named token reference another token. The format permits alias chains but prohibits circular references; the resolver also requires aliases to point to the correct type. (high confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/format/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes · also: https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
- [statement] A mode can keep a semantic token name stable while changing its value for a context such as light or dark appearance. The DTCG resolver describes conditional token values using sets and modifiers. (high confidence) — https://www.contentful.com/blog/design-token-system/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes · also: https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/
- [statement] A resolver document describes conditional values but requires external inputs to select contexts. Conforming tools validate inputs against declared modifiers and allowed context values. (low confidence) — https://www.designtokens.org/tr/2025.10/resolver/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Design token interoperability, themes and modes
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group defines DesignOps as coordinating people, processes, and craft to increase design impact at scale; its operational remit includes documenting delivery processes and defining design quality and completion criteria. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/design-operations-101/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] Preserve design rationale alongside the implementation reference: Figma’s handoff guide describes linking specs to problem definitions, research, and iterations; Cegid recommends recording important implementation decisions and trade-offs for future work. (medium confidence) — https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/
- [statement] Define implementation-review responsibilities explicitly. The designer-developer collaboration review reports unclear responsibility boundaries and loss of UX involvement in development decisions; Cegid advocates joint decisions on emerging edge cases and review of implemented features before QA. (medium confidence) — https://arxiv.org/html/2501.11748v1 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/
- [statement] Modeinspect proposes a concrete design-QA workflow: the screen’s designer reviews the preview build before merge, while the engineer reviews code and retains the merge gate. Its checklist extends beyond layout to interaction states, responsive behavior, accessibility, content, and motion. This is a vendor’s proposed division of work, not a universal ownership rule. (low confidence) — https://modeinspect.com/blog/design-qa · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] In Modeinspect’s distinction, visual regression compares a build with an approved previous-build baseline, whereas design QA compares the implementation with design intent; an unchanged baseline can therefore preserve an original design mismatch. (low confidence) — https://modeinspect.com/blog/design-qa · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] Treat implementation feedback as continuing design work: Cegid recommends joint user-story review, edge-case decisions, and feedback in both directions; Figma’s guide describes early developer collaboration and visibility into the iterations behind design decisions. (medium confidence) — https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://www.figma.com/best-practices/guide-to-developer-handoff/
- [statement] Nielsen Norman Group recommends recording UX debt and prioritizing it by user impact, frequency, journey location, and effort. Its alternatives include a labelled backlog or a separate prioritization sheet, followed by deliberate capacity for repayment; the article acknowledges that teams may consciously accept debt for release constraints. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-debt/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] Specify behavior beyond the default screen, including empty states and behavior between screen widths. The developer interviews identify these gaps, and Modeinspect identifies missing states and responsive decisions as sources of implementation drift. (medium confidence) — https://zeroheight.com/blog/what-do-developers-want-in-a-design-handoff-we-asked-them/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://modeinspect.com/blog/design-qa
- [statement] Cegid recommends recording important implementation trade-offs so later iterations retain the reasoning, and reviewing implemented features before QA to catch accessibility, interaction, and usability issues. (low confidence) — https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA
- [statement] A delivery feedback loop should combine implementation feedback with experience review: Cegid describes developers surfacing technical opportunities and designers spotting usability issues; NN/g recommends recurring product-team reviews and using user feedback to uncover UX debt. (medium confidence) — https://composedesign.ila.cegid.com/blog/bridging-the-gap-collaboration-between-designer-and-developers-after-handoff/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-debt/
- [statement] Do not equate documented criteria or stable screenshots with complete quality assurance. GDS warns that accessibility acceptance criteria alone do not make a service accessible; Modeinspect warns that visual regression can preserve a baseline that never matched the intended design. (medium confidence) — https://insidegovuk.blog.gov.uk/2018/01/24/improving-accessibility-with-accessibility-acceptance-criteria/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, DesignOps, developer handoff and design QA · also: https://modeinspect.com/blog/design-qa
- [statement] Recruit across the target population’s backgrounds and abilities, and track which segments have been missed; choose recruitment criteria using the product’s users, research objectives and likely barriers. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recruiting-screening-research-candidates/
- [statement] Screeners should establish relevant experience without unnecessary exclusion rules. Nielsen Norman Group recommends avoiding questions that reveal the desired answer and reviewing responses from both qualified and disqualified candidates. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recruiting-screening-research-candidates/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Obtain consent through understandable information and a voluntary decision: explain the study purpose, activities, data use and sharing, recording, and the right to stop; allow time for questions. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Make consent accessible in both language and format. GOV.UK offers reading aloud, assistive-technology-compatible digital forms and recorded verbal consent as practical alternatives; Indeed recommends checking understanding in participants’ own words. (medium confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://indeed.design/article/three-basic-principles-of-ethical-research-that-ux-can-take-from-academia/
- [statement] Keep evidence of what each participant consented to and match that record to the corresponding research data. (low confidence) — https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/getting-users-consent-for-research · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Minimise personal data collection and protect confidentiality; removing names alone may leave participants identifiable through characteristics or quotations, especially in small recruitment pools. (medium confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Prepare a response for participant distress or unsafe situations, allow rest and consider debriefing; ethical care extends beyond obtaining a signed consent form. (medium confidence) — https://indeed.design/article/three-basic-principles-of-ethical-research-that-ux-can-take-from-academia/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/
- [statement] Counterpoint on incentives: in a biomedical research ethics analysis, the authors argue against conventional conservatism toward payment and ask whether participants are paid enough. This is an attributed ethical argument, not an empirical estimate for UX or a universal payment rule. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5728432/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Make participation accessible through usable research tools and alternative information formats, and budget for requested access support such as captioning, interpretation and attendant reimbursement. (medium confidence) — https://tetralogical.com/blog/2022/08/01/inclusive-user-research-recruiting-participants/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics · also: https://www.section508.gov/develop/usability-testing-with-people-with-disabilities/
- [statement] Cambridge’s toolkit advises that participants should still receive the offered incentive if they withdraw after beginning the study. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Cambridge warns that removing names alone may not anonymize study data: characteristics, small recruitment pools and quotations can still identify participants. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Cambridge advises consulting specific ethical guidance for children, people with dementia and research methods where ordinary informed consent may not be feasible; its introductory guidance is not a complete protocol for those situations. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Cambridge’s toolkit recommends reporting participants fairly and accurately, listening to what they say without preconceived ideas. (low confidence) — https://www.inclusivedesigntoolkit.com/ethics/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Inclusive UX research recruitment, consent and ethics
- [statement] Treat a locale as more than a language: regional conventions affect dates, currencies, units and other interaction details. (medium confidence) — https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/locale/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://simplelocalize.io/blog/posts/ui-localization-best-practices/
- [statement] For RTL interfaces, mirror navigation order and directional icons, and align translated RTL text appropriately. Right-aligning text alone does not describe the required layout changes. (medium confidence) — https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/code-quality/coding-style/rtl_guidelines.html
- [statement] Preserve the reading direction of numbers and embedded LTR words such as URLs inside an RTL interface; do not reverse their characters with the surrounding layout. (medium confidence) — https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/
- [statement] Apply mirroring selectively: Mozilla excludes direction-neutral icons, product logos and video/audio controls; Material likewise excludes non-directional icons and media playback controls. (medium confidence) — https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/code-quality/coding-style/rtl_guidelines.html · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html
- [statement] Allow translated text to reflow and avoid tightly constrained fixed-width containers. Expansion depends on the string, and contraction can also disturb layouts; one universal expansion allowance is insufficient. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Validate actual script typography, including font coverage, accents, line height and mixed-script alignment. Character counts alone do not determine the space needed by translated text. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/alreq/, https://simplelocalize.io/blog/posts/ui-localization-best-practices/
- [statement] Test localized experiences with users in the target markets early and after launch. NN/g reports that domestic testing can miss culturally specific issues and features international users rely on. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-international-usability-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Combine visual QA for each locale, manual RTL testing and native-speaker review; SimpleLocalize explicitly includes all three in its localization checklist. (low confidence) — https://simplelocalize.io/blog/posts/ui-localization-best-practices/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Practitioner guidance differs on dates: Exadel recommends an international date format for RTL interfaces, while SimpleLocalize recommends local date formats. These are attributed recommendations, not evidence that one format suits every Arabic-speaking user. (low confidence) — https://exadel.com/news/localization-testing-tips-and-tricks-for-rtl-language-websites-and-apps · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://simplelocalize.io/blog/posts/ui-localization-best-practices/
- [statement] W3C distinguishes internationalization, which enables localization through product design and development, from localization, which adapts a product to the language, cultural and other requirements of a target locale. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-i18n · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Localization extends beyond translating words: review number, date and time formats, currency, sorting, address and contact formats, and script readability; locale conventions can differ within the same language. (medium confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-i18n · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/locale/
- [statement] Mixed-direction inline phrases can misplace neutral punctuation or adjacent numbers and can reorder logically separate phrases. W3C identifies URLs, phone numbers, addresses and names as common examples that require attention. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/inline-bidi-markup/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Mirror back and forward navigation to preserve reading-order meaning in RTL interfaces. Preserve controls that indicate an actual physical direction or point to a specific onscreen area. (medium confidence) — https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/right-to-left · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl
- [statement] Selective mirroring preserves meaning: Material Design keeps media playback controls and clockwise clock or circular-progress symbols unchanged; Apple also advises preserving logos, universal marks and real-world object icons unless the object communicates direction. (medium confidence) — https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/right-to-left
- [statement] Material Design 3 explicitly scopes mirroring by locale: graphs and charts retain LTR directionality for Persian and Urdu, while Hebrew timelines, media controls and linear progress indicators retain LTR directionality. (low confidence) — https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html
- [statement] Plan for translated text to change length. W3C recommends flexible layouts, reflow, avoiding small fixed-width containers, and keeping font size and line height adaptable. Its examples do not justify one universal expansion allowance for every string. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Character count alone does not predict translated layout size. W3C describes wider glyphs and greater line-height requirements in non-Latin scripts; typography review must include horizontal and vertical space. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/International/articles/article-text-size/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] For Arabic-script typography, verify cursive joining and diacritic positioning with the intended font. W3C describes letters joining their neighbors and multiple diacritics attaching to one base character using font-defined shapes or positions. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/alreq/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Validate with people in the intended market early. Nielsen Norman Group reports that international testing can expose language-switcher findability and other problems that domestic testing misses, and recommends testing before a new-market launch. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-international-usability-testing/ · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design
- [statement] Include gestures in RTL interaction review. Material Design 3 says horizontal swipes and the side from which swipe actions are revealed should mirror their LTR counterparts. (low confidence) — https://m3.material.io/foundations/layout/bidirectionality-rtl · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Internationalization, localization and RTL interaction design · also: https://m2.material.io/design/usability/bidirectionality.html
- [statement] Co-design gives participants influence over problems, ideas and decisions. Asking for feedback while others retain decisions is consultation; research participation alone does not establish co-design. (high confidence) — https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.thinknpc.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Co-design-guidance-July-2019.pdf, https://d-lab.mit.edu/news-blog/blog/co-creating-more-equitable-world-transformative-benefits-participatory-design
- [statement] Budget for participants’ time and the costs of participation. Choose payment arrangements that work for participants, and include access support, suitable venues and accessible materials in the budget. (medium confidence) — https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://d-lab.mit.edu/news-blog/blog/co-creating-more-equitable-world-transformative-benefits-participatory-design
- [statement] Adapt workshop conditions and materials to participants, and revise them from feedback. Reported failures include rooms without microphones or loudspeakers, inaccessible materials and presentations that move too quickly; the practitioner guide recommends describing visual aids and providing different ways to contribute. (medium confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Make decisions traceable through written collaboration terms, shared workshop summaries, and explicit communication of design limitations and trade-offs. This is an operational synthesis of the sources’ transparency guidance, not a prescribed decision-log format. (medium confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Attendance alone is insufficient evidence of meaningful influence. In the empirical study, participants described being invited without having their input taken into account; the accessible co-design guide recommends being honest about what can change and the barriers to change. (medium confidence) — https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952 · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf
- [statement] Do not promise that co-design is always the best or cheapest approach: MIT D-Lab says it can cost more than alternatives and is not a silver bullet; Mural identifies time, resource, decision-making and equitable-participation challenges. (medium confidence) — https://d-lab.mit.edu/news-blog/blog/co-creating-more-equitable-world-transformative-benefits-participatory-design · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.mural.co/blog/co-design-method
- [statement] Choose meaningful participatory roles: Alfred Health recommends people with lived experience on the project team and as workshop co-leaders or co-facilitators, with support and training; NPC also proposes participants helping decide what and how to evaluate. (high confidence) — https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://www.thinknpc.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/Co-design-guidance-July-2019.pdf
- [statement] Budget appropriate compensation for participants’ time and expertise. Alfred Health recommends flexible payment arrangements that work for each person; participants in the empirical framework study described reimbursement as recognition of equal partnership. (high confidence) — https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design · also: https://sjdr.se/articles/10.16993/sjdr.952
- [statement] For online co-design workshops, Alfred Health recommends accessible agendas and joining instructions in advance, sufficient time for activities and questions, description of visual aids, and multiple ways to contribute, including speaking, chat and visual cards. These are facilitation recommendations, not proof that any particular platform is accessible to everyone. (low confidence) — https://www.alfredhealth.org.au/images/resources/patient-resources/SPEAK_Co-design_Guide_PRINT.pdf · keywords: UI/UX design: inclusive systems, Participatory design and accessible co-design
- [statement] Keep a traceable feedback loop: NPC recommends explaining what the team heard and changed in response to participants.
